steps.say: A small back-of-skull in some people lets the cerebellar tips slip below the great opening. Half develop a fluid cavity in the cord, and coughing brings a bursting headache at the back. Downward-beating eye jerks and wasting of the hand muscles complete the picture.
steps.tx: **Chiari I** (tonsillar descent disorder) means **5 mm descent** (five millimetre tonsil drop) beyond the foramen magnum with a small posterior fossa, half with syringomyelia. It presents with occipital **cough headache** (bursting pain on coughing), **downbeat nystagmus** (downward eye jerks) and hand wasting, and about **50 percent** (fifty percent) carry a cord cavity needing surveillance.

vis.alt: Sagittal diagram comparing normal brain and spinal cord anatomy at the craniocervical junction with Chiari I and Chiari II malformations, showing cerebellar tonsil displacement and a spinal syrinx.
vis.caption: Chiari I and II with tonsil descent and spinal syrinx at the junction. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Headache with a cord cavity or pressure on the brainstem earns an operation that opens the bone and widens the covering. Harmless low-lying tonsils found by chance are simply watched. Operating on every incidental dip would harm more than help.
steps.tx: When Chiari I causes symptoms with a syrinx or brainstem pressure, **foramen magnum decompression** (great-hole opening) with **duraplasty** (covering widening) is the answer. Silent chance-found low tonsils (**incidental ectopia**) are watched instead. The operation restores fluid flow around the junction, so symptoms plus syrinx mark the surgical case and silence marks the watched one.

steps.say: The second type travels with an open spine in the newborn and a squeezed, beaked midbrain. Most of these babies need fluid diversion, while opening the back of the skull is reserved for those with breathing and swallowing trouble from brainstem squash.
steps.tx: **Chiari II** (open-spine hindbrain disorder) accompanies **myelomeningocele** (open spinal sac) with a small posterior fossa, **beaked tectum** (pointed midbrain roof) and medullary kinking. Most need shunting for hydrocephalus, with decompression reserved for symptomatic brainstem compression, since closing the back defect and diverting fluid come first in the newborn.

steps.say: A fluid cavity hollowing the centre of the cord steals pain feeling while sparing light touch, classically in a cape across the shoulders. Burnt hands without pain and crumbling joints follow. The wasted small hand muscles point to the lower neck.
steps.tx: **Syringomyelia** (cord-centre fluid cavity) produces cape-like **dissociated sensory loss** (pain lost, touch spared) with intrinsic hand wasting. Painless **Charcot joints** (destroyed joints from unfelt injuries) follow, and the **spinothalamic** (pain-temperature tract) pattern across shoulders and hands localises the cavity to the cervical cord.

steps.say: Draining the skull opening usually collapses the cord cavity on its own by restoring flow. Direct tubes into the cavity are reserved for cavities walled off by old infection or injury. Fix the flow first and the syrinx is often gone for good.
steps.tx: Most syrinxes resolve after Chiari decompression restores **cisternal flow** (fluid movement at the junction), with direct **syrinx shunt** (cavity drainage tube) reserved for post-traumatic or post-infective **loculated cavity** (walled-off fluid pockets). Flow restoration first avoids a cord tube, since shunting a communicating cavity treats the consequence, not the block.

nodes.label: Cavity collapses; shunt only loculated ones

steps.say: In some patients the peg of the second vertebra migrates upward into the skull opening, pressing the brainstem and lower nerves. Two classic skull lines mark how far it has risen. Long-tract stiffness and tongue wasting follow the squeeze.
steps.tx: In **basilar invagination** (peg rising into the skull) the odontoid climbs past the **Chamberlain line** (palate to skull-base line) and the **McGregor line** (second palate to skull-base line) into the great hole. That **odontoid invagination** (peg compressing the brainstem) causes long-tract signs and lower nerve palsies that posterior reduction-fixation reverses.

steps.say: Modern teaching blames a loose joint between the first two vertebrae for most upward migration. Fixing those two bones from behind with joint lifting corrects even cases once thought to need drilling through the mouth. Reducible slips never need the transoral route.
steps.tx: Goel doctrine treats most basilar invagination as **atlantoaxial instability** (loose **C1-C2** (first-second vertebrae) joint), fixing **C1-C2** posteriorly with **joint distraction** (spacer lifting) even without transoral odontoidectomy in reducible cases. Stabilising the loose joint lets the odontoid settle back down, sparing the mouth-splitting front operation.

steps.say: The worst junction injury tears the skull from the spine entirely and is usually fatal at the roadside. Survivors can never be trusted in a collar because torn ligaments do not heal. Urgent fusion from skull to neck is the only safe answer.
steps.tx: Traumatic **atlanto-occipital dislocation** (skull-spine separation) per **Traynelis** (displacement direction grading) patterns is highly lethal. Survivors get urgent **occipitocervical fusion** (skull-to-spine metal joining) because the ligamentous injury never heals in a collar, and any delay risks fatal re-displacement with the next small movement.
